headline: Where worldviews share ground and where they split
intro: Each sphere is an idea, drawn from the public writing and talks of the people on the map, on AI and society. Each diamond is a person. Select someone and the structure they stand on lights up.

Habermas called the background we reason from the lifeworld: it mostly goes unseen until something brings a piece of it into question. This map tries to do that on purpose, so that people can reason about the ground they stand on, and test whether they would sign how they are described.

schools.label: AI as a new kind of risk
schools.note: They see a real risk of human extinction from advanced AI, want binding rules and early work on control, and don't think public fear or AI's promises are overblown.

schools.label: AI as a tool to govern
schools.note: They see AI as a tool rather than a new kind of mind, put today's harms ahead of superintelligence, and want binding rules because how technology changes society is a collective choice.

schools.label: Market optimists
schools.note: Public fear of AI outruns the evidence, market-driven technology is good for people, and strict regulation or a slowdown would do more harm than good.

schools.label: A new mind on its own course
schools.note: A loose group: they see AI as a new kind of mind whose course isn't simply set by collective choice, and back pushing ahead of China.

lenses.label: Accelerationism and AI safety
lenses.note: These camps were chosen by name, and the people in them sit in several measured schools.

findings.title: Accelerationism and AI safety share a picture of AI, and split on what to do
findings.body: Both sides hold that intelligence can run on silicon and that capable AI has no built-in reason to care for us. The split sharpens upward: at the action layer they oppose each other on 4 of 5 shared idea families. They also split at the roots, over whether collective choice can steer technology and whether intelligence can pair with any goal. E/acc does not form its own school here.

findings.title: The AI safety and AI ethics feud sits at the very bottom
findings.body: AI safety people and AI critics agree on all 6 shared families about knowing and all 8 about the world, and on 6 of 7 about action. They split on what language models are. If they could settle that one question, or set it aside, much of their conflict has less to stand on.

findings.title: Some alliances cross the usual lines
findings.body: Hawley sits with Bender, Gebru and Hao in 65% to 90% of reruns: Hawley and Bender share 18 ideas and oppose on none measured. Thiel and Karp share 5 ideas with no opposition yet rarely group together (7%), because most of what they write is about different things.

findings.title: Popular links can vanish, as Yarvin and Vance do
findings.body: They share one idea in what they argue and land in the same school in 2% of reruns. This sample can't rule out influence, and it shows no shared structure.

words: The same word can carry a different world. This compares the sentences each group builds around a word. A larger gap means the surroundings differ more. It catches a change of subject as well as a change of meaning, so read the examples before trusting a gap.
belonging: Habermas held that we cohere by giving reasons. Karp's dissertation argued that jargon binds groups by licensing aggression. These widely held ideas have the fewest argument links. That could mean they mostly mark membership, or that our link readers missed their reasons, so this is a lead to test.

p: We read public works by every person on the map: their own essays, talks and interviews. Each claim needs an exact quote, then passes code checks and a local entailment model. Positions on the 24 fingerprint statements were then re-read from the full texts by two blind readers, and only positions two independent readings support are shown.

Readers merged claims into shared ideas, each placed in a layer: being, knowing, values, world or action. Every holding then got a blind second reading, and we kept only what both readings agreed on. Saying nothing about an idea counts as missing, never as disagreement.

The layers draw on Apostel and Aerts's worldview components, Bourdieu's doxa and Habermas's lifeworld. Links use argument theory: Toulmin, Walton and ASPIC+. These are proposals, and the framing itself is open to dispute.

Thinkers rarely address the same exact claim. Only about a tenth of person and idea pairs have a recorded stance. So people are compared over 40 families of related ideas, with shared ground removed. Height is the layer and is fixed. Links pull supporting ideas together and push opposed ones apart, around measured positions.

Nobody placed here has seen this or agreed to it. All of it is provisional machine reading, and no person has ratified it. Each person is read from about three works, so dates mean first appearance in this sample and cannot show change over time. Twenty-seven hand-picked people show a pattern, not a population. School names are working labels, and the people named should replace them.

self: Worldviews have layers, and some assumptions sit deeper than others.
People's public words are fair evidence of what they hold.
Seeing a shared root can help people who disagree.
Describing a view in terms its holders would sign is a good, and agreement is not required.
Disagreement between camps deserves to be mapped, and the middle has no special standing.

c1.label: AI as a new kind of risk
c1.note: They see a real risk of human extinction from advanced AI, want binding rules and early work on control, and don't think public fear or AI's promises are overblown.

c1.1.label: Slow it down and govern it
c1.1.note: They want the most powerful AI deliberately slowed and bound by government rules, because they don't trust companies to make it safe on their own.

c1.1.1.label: Public authority over AI
c1.1.1.note: How technology reshapes society is a collective choice, and strict regulation now would not do more harm than good.

c1.1.1.1.label: Sanders and Elmore
c1.1.1.1.note: Closest of all here: AI should serve people, and political authority should rest with the public.

c1.1.2.label: Researchers for state oversight
c1.1.2.note: The gravest danger is autonomous superintelligence rather than today's misuse, so the state should direct frontier AI and the most capable models should not be released openly.

c1.1.2.1.label: Russell and Bengio
c1.1.2.1.note: Closest of all here: they also see AI-made content as a threat to shared truth, and would never let AI decide on its own to use lethal force.

c1.2.label: Build it, but under rules
c1.2.note: They take advanced AI's promise seriously and don't think building smarter-than-human machines is wrong in itself, but want binding government rules and early work on control.

c1.2.1.label: Hassabis and Mowshowitz
c1.2.1.note: Closest of all here: extinction risk is real, public fear isn't overblown, and the most capable models shouldn't be released openly.

c1.2.2.label: Clark and Suleyman
c1.2.2.note: Closest of all here: AI is a new kind of mind, and earlier technologies are not a reliable guide to it.

c1.3.label: Extinction risk, no race
c1.3.note: They see a real risk of extinction and want control worked out early; most reject racing China and back sharing AI's gains directly with citizens.

c1.3.1.label: Yudkowsky and Musk
c1.3.1.note: Closest of all here: AI companies need outside rules, and on hard questions they would follow a careful argument over the average of opinion.

c1.4.label: The risk is real, and so is the promise
c1.4.note: They see a real risk of extinction, reject the idea that AI's promises are hype, and want control worked out well before it's needed.

c1.4.1.label: Hinton and MacAskill
c1.4.1.note: Closest of all here: the bigger danger is autonomous superintelligence, not only today's misuse.

c2.label: AI as a tool to govern
c2.note: They see AI as a tool rather than a new kind of mind, put today's harms ahead of superintelligence, and want binding rules because how technology changes society is a collective choice.

c2.1.label: Public control of AI
c2.1.note: Political authority should rest with the public, AI shouldn't concentrate power in a few companies, and productivity gains won't reach workers without new policy.

c2.1.1.label: Pay creators, share power
c2.1.1.note: AI companies should pay the people whose work they train on, and the promises made for AI are oversold.

c2.1.1.1.label: A say for workers
c2.1.1.1.note: Closest of all here: workers should have a legal say in how AI is used where they work.

c2.2.label: Today's harms, oversold promises
c2.2.note: AI's promises are oversold, the dangers that matter most come from how it is deployed now, and companies won't make it safe without outside rules.

c2.2.1.label: Whittaker and Gebru
c2.2.1.note: Closest of all here: they reject the extinction-risk framing and expect AI on its current course to concentrate power in a few companies.

c3.label: Market optimists
c3.note: Public fear of AI outruns the evidence, market-driven technology is good for people, and strict regulation or a slowdown would do more harm than good.

c3.1.label: Keep the state out
c3.1.note: Market competition limits harm, AI development shouldn't be directed by the state, and strict regulation now would do more harm than good.

c3.1.1.label: Verdon and Cruz
c3.1.1.note: Closest of all here: companies don't need outside rules to make AI safe, but should be liable when their products harm people.

c3.2.label: History as a guide
c3.2.note: Earlier general-purpose technologies are a valid guide to AI, its promise is real, and it shouldn't be slowed.

c3.3.label: Serve people, lead on AI
c3.3.note: AI should serve people rather than surpass them, the real dangers come from misuse rather than superintelligence, and rivalry with China is a reason to push ahead.

c3.3.1.label: Andreessen and LeCun
c3.3.1.note: Closest of all here: they see no real risk of extinction and oppose binding rules on frontier developers.

c3.4.label: Yarvin and Rao
c3.4.note: Closest here: they see no real risk of extinction and think public fear outruns the evidence.

c4.label: A new mind on its own course
c4.note: A loose group: they see AI as a new kind of mind whose course isn't simply set by collective choice, and back pushing ahead of China.

c4.1.label: Ball and Land
c4.1.note: Closest here: frontier AI shouldn't be slowed, and building smarter-than-human machines isn't wrong in itself.
